Michigan property tax FAQ

When does the Michigan board of review meet?

The statute cited above says the second Monday in March, with alternative start dates a city or township may authorize.

How are Michigan property taxes calculated before you sell?

Michigan assesses property at 50 percent of its true cash value, and that half-value figure is the state equalized value (SEV). Tax is not charged on SEV directly. It is charged on taxable value, which for each parcel is the lesser of two numbers: last year's taxable value (less losses) multiplied by 1.05 or the inflation rate, whichever is smaller, plus additions, or the current SEV (MCL 211.27a).

This is the Proposal A cap, and it is why two neighboring houses of equal market value can carry very different bills. A long-time owner usually pays on a taxable value well below SEV. The cushion belongs to the owner's tenure, not to the parcel, and that single point shapes most Michigan sale-day tax surprises.

  • SEV is half of the assessor's estimate of true cash value.
  • Taxable value grows slowly while the same owner holds the parcel.
  • The millage rate set by each local taxing unit is applied to taxable value to produce the bill.

What happens to taxable value when the house sells?

A transfer of ownership resets taxable value. For the calendar year after the transfer, taxable value becomes the SEV, and the 5-percent-or-inflation cap then applies again from that new base (MCL 211.27a(3) and (4)). The statute defines transfer broadly: a deed, a land contract, certain trust changes, and a distribution under a will or by intestacy all count.

An heir who is the decedent's spouse, parent, child, sibling or grandchild can take a home without the reset, provided it stays residential (MCL 211.27a(6)(f)). A land contract is treated as a transfer when it is signed, and the later deed does not trigger a second reset.

The new owner files a State Tax Commission form with the local assessing office, listing the parties, the date, the real price paid and the parcel number or legal description, and the deadline is 45 days after the transfer (MCL 211.27a(10)). Deed recordings are also passed to the assessor at least monthly, so the reset does not wait on that paperwork.

When does the board of review meet, and how do you appeal in Michigan?

The first step is the local board of review. It meets the second Monday in March, and a city or township may choose the Tuesday or Wednesday after that as the starting date. Its opening session starts no earlier than 9 a.m. and no later than 3 p.m., lasts six hours or more, and the board sits 12 hours across that week, three of them in the evening. (MCL 211.30).

An owner or an agent can ask for a corrected assessed or taxable value, and the board must correct it if sufficient cause is shown. A nonresident can protest by letter, and a township or city may also allow resident protests by letter. The board mails its written decision, along with a notice about the tribunal, no later than the first Monday of June.

The Michigan Tax Tribunal hears the next level. For a house, the petition goes in by July 31 of the tax year, and the same date covers agricultural and timber-cutover land. Commercial, industrial and developmental real property, plus related personal property, has an earlier May 31 date. Other matters give 35 days from the final decision. A residential valuation case generally starts with a board of review protest. Disputes limited to arithmetic mistakes on a bill get 60 days from the treasurer's mailing (MCL 205.735a).

How does the principal residence exemption work when you sell?

The principal residence exemption (PRE) removes the local school operating tax from an owner's home. An owner claims it by filing a Principal Residence Exemption Affidavit, Form 2368, with the city or township assessor. Filing by June 1 lowers the summer levy, while a filing between June 2 and November 1 starts with the winter levy (Treasury PRE claim requirements).

The reverse step matters at sale. Once the home is no longer the owner's principal residence, Form 2602, a Request to Rescind, goes to the assessor inside a 90-day window. Filing late costs $5 a day, capped at $200, and the roll drops the exemption at year end of the filing year.

The same duty reaches other cases. After an owner dies, the personal representative or trustee files it. After a divorce, the departing spouse files it. After a lender forecloses, the former borrower files it once the home is vacated. Forms come from closing agents, assessors and the Treasury website.

What if the property taxes are not paid?

Township and city treasurers send the bills and collect first. A summer levy is a lien and falls due July 1, and interest runs on anything collected after September 14. Whatever is still unpaid on March 1 goes to the county as delinquent (MCL 211.44a).

A collecting unit may add an administration fee of up to 1 percent to a bill paid before mid-February. From February 15 until the delinquent return, the city or township may authorize that fee plus a 3 percent late charge (MCL 211.44).

The serious step comes a year later. Each March 1, parcels that were delinquent for a full prior 12 months forfeit to the county treasurer, and a $175 fee is added. A certificate is recorded at the deeds office inside 45 days. Redemption means paying everything owed plus extra interest of one-half percent a month, and it is open through the March 31 that follows the foreclosure judgment, or 21 days after judgment if the case is contested (MCL 211.78g). A seller with back taxes should request a written payoff figure from the county treasurer long before then.

EventRuleSource
Board of reviewSecond Monday in March, or the Tuesday or Wednesday afterMCL 211.30
Tribunal, residentialPetition by July 31 of the tax yearMCL 205.735a
Summer taxDue July 1; interest after September 14MCL 211.44a
ForfeitureMarch 1 after 12 months or more delinquentMCL 211.78g
Transfer noticeBuyer notifies assessor within 45 daysMCL 211.27a

What should a Michigan seller check before closing?

Start with the parcel's tax history and work outward. Closing agents ask for these same items, and a gap is cheaper to close early.

  • Confirm with the township or city treasurer which bills are paid, then check with the county office whether any year went delinquent.
  • Check the exemption status with the assessor, and send in the rescission form within 90 days of moving out.
  • Warn the buyer that the year after closing, taxable value moves up to SEV, so last year's bill understates what comes next.
  • To contest the assessment on a house, plan for the March board first and the July 31 tribunal date after it.
  • For an inherited house, find out whether the family exception holds the old taxable value before the heirs choose between keeping and selling.

Owners several years behind should act before forfeiture. After it, the parcel sits with the county treasurer, the foreclosing governmental unit takes possession only on the April 1 after judgment, and redemption ends at the March 31 cutoff.

More questions about Michigan Property Tax Guide

When does the Michigan board of review meet?

The week of the second Monday in March. Some cities and townships open one or two days later, on the Tuesday or Wednesday, and every board owes 12 hours of hearings that week, with three after 6 p.m.

When must a homeowner petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal?

Your petition must be filed by July 31 of the tax year. Residential cases generally begin with a board of review protest. Commercial and industrial real property follow an earlier May 31 date.

Do Michigan property taxes go up when a house is sold?

Often. A transfer of ownership sets taxable value equal to SEV for the next calendar year, wiping out the Proposal A gap the seller built up. The buyer reports the transfer to the assessor within 45 days.

How do I remove the principal residence exemption after selling?

Send Form 2602 to the local assessor within 90 days of ceasing to live there as your principal residence. Missing the window triggers $5 per day, with a $200 ceiling.

When does Michigan property go into forfeiture for unpaid taxes?

Each March 1, after taxes have gone unpaid for the prior 12 months or longer. The parcel is forfeited to the county treasurer for the amount owed, and redemption by full payment stays possible through the following March 31 after the foreclosure judgment.

Michigan exempts a principal residence from the local school operating tax if the owner files the affidavit.

What the official sources say

  • A principal residence is exempt from the tax levied by a local school district for school operating purposes if the owner files an affidavit. (MCL 211.7cc(1); source)
  • The exemption lasts until December 31 of the year the property is transferred or is no longer a principal residence. (MCL 211.7cc(4); source)
  • An owner may retain the exemption up to 3 tax years on a former residence if it is not occupied, is for sale, not leased, and not used for business, by filing a conditional rescission form. (MCL 211.7cc(5); source)
  • Form 2368 Principal Residence Exemption Affidavit is filed with the city/township assessor; deadlines June 1 (summer levy) and November 1 (winter levy). (Treasury: PRE Claim Requirement; source)
  • A principal residence exemption exempts the home from local school operating millage, up to 18 mills. (Treasury: Principal Residence Exemption; source)

What we could not confirm

  • Anything beyond the statute text on the Treasury page.

Michigan homestead exemption FAQ

How do I claim the principal residence exemption?

File the affidavit with the local assessor by the deadlines cited above.

What is the principal residence exemption in Michigan?

It is a break on the school operating part of your property tax bill. Michigan's Treasury describes it as exempting an owner's principal residence from the local school operating millage, up to 18 mills (Treasury PRE page). The statute behind it is MCL 211.7cc.

People often call it the homestead exemption, but Michigan keeps the two ideas apart. The Homestead Property Tax Credit is a separate credit claimed on an income tax return. The exemption discussed here is claimed with the local assessor and shows up on the tax roll.

A principal residence is the one place where an owner has a true, fixed, and permanent home to which the owner intends to return whenever absent. It also reaches the owner's unoccupied residential or timber-cutover land that adjoins the dwelling and is owned and occupied by the owner (MCL 211.7dd(c)).

Who counts as an owner for the exemption?

Only an individual who holds a documented ownership interest. Treasury's ownership guidance says verbal agreements do not create an interest, and the person claiming carries the burden of proof. The groups it lists as eligible are below.

  • A person who owns the property, including a partial owner.
  • A land contract purchaser under a written contract that the seller signed.
  • A holder of a life estate, who is treated as a partial owner.
  • A beneficiary who receives ownership rights under a will, a trust, or intestate succession.
  • A grantor who placed the home in a revocable trust or a qualified personal residence trust.
  • A cooperative housing corporation or a registered life care facility.

An LLC, a corporation, a shareholder of a corporation, and a sole member of an LLC do not qualify. A trust is not itself an owner, though its grantor or beneficiaries may be. In a married couple that files a joint Michigan return, only one exemption is allowed (MCL 211.7cc(3)).

When and where do I file the affidavit?

File Form 2368, the Principal Residence Exemption Affidavit, with the assessor for the city or township where the home sits. The statute sets June 1 for the summer levy and November 1 for the winter levy (MCL 211.7cc(2)). A valid affidavit filed by June 1 reduces that year's bill starting with the summer levy. One filed from June 2 through November 1 reduces it starting with the winter levy.

The affidavit states that you own and occupy the property on the signing date and have not claimed a substantially similar break in another state. Claiming both brings a $500 penalty. Treasury also warns that a false claim can bring perjury charges, with penalties that include up to a year in jail and fines of $1,000 to $5,000 (MCL 211.120).

Closing agents and local assessors hand out the forms, and Treasury also posts them. The statute adds that a closing statement preparer who skips the forms is not legally liable for it, so the seller and buyer should ask for them.

What if I missed a deadline?

You can still file. Treasury says the owner may file Form 2368 with the local assessor at any time during the year, and the assessor may grant the exemption back through the current year and the three years before it, provided the owner met the requirements on June 1 or November 1 of each year claimed. If the owner has died, the estate can file for the same period.

Since July 11, 2022, the July and December Boards of Review no longer have authority to grant late claims. Only the assessor does, so go to the assessor's office rather than waiting for a board hearing.

Which dates and rules matter most?

Principal residence exemption timing rules, from MCL 211.7cc and Treasury guidance
EventRuleWhere it comes from
Claim for summer levyAffidavit on or before June 1MCL 211.7cc(2)
Claim for winter levyAffidavit on or before November 1MCL 211.7cc(2)
Home stops being principal residenceRescind within 90 days using Form 2602MCL 211.7cc(5)
Late rescission$5 per day, capped at $200MCL 211.7cc(5)
Rescission takes effectRemoved as of December 31 of the filing yearMCL 211.7cc(15)
Appeal of a denial35 days to the Michigan tax tribunalMCL 211.7cc(13)

How does the exemption work for two parcels, a duplex, or a split lot?

Each parcel needs its own affidavit. Treasury's example is an owner whose home sits on one parcel and whose contiguous residential land is a second parcel: both need Form 2368. When a parcel is split or combined, the new parcel numbers mean a fresh affidavit.

If the home is one unit of a multiple-unit dwelling, or a dwelling within a mixed-use building, the owner claims only the share of taxable value used as the principal residence, in the manner Treasury prescribes (MCL 211.7cc(16)). A landlord who lives in one side of a duplex therefore claims that side only. Ask the local assessor how the portion is measured before you file.

What must a seller do with the exemption?

The exemption lasts until December 31 of the year the property is transferred, or until it stops being a principal residence (MCL 211.7cc(4)). Within 90 days after you stop using the home as your principal residence you must file Form 2602 with the local tax collecting unit. Treasury lists several cases where rescission is still required: the owner dies, a spouse leaves after a divorce, or the owner moves out during a foreclosure redemption period.

There is one holding option if you moved and the house is for sale. An owner who claims the exemption on a new current residence can keep it on the old home for up to 3 tax years by filing a conditional rescission form, as long as the old home is unoccupied, listed for sale, not leased, and not used for business. Lease it and the local unit denies the conditional rescission back to the prior December 31.

An owner who moved into a nursing home or assisted living facility may keep the exemption if the home stays owned, no new principal residence is set up, the home is maintained, and it is not leased or used for business.

How are denials, audits, and back taxes handled?

An assessor who believes the home is not the owner's principal residence can deny a new or existing claim in writing, for the current year and up to the three years before. The owner has 35 days from the notice date to appeal to the residential and small claims division of the Michigan tax tribunal, and does not have to pay the disputed tax to appeal. Counties can elect to audit claims, and Treasury audits annually in counties that do not.

Back taxes carry interest at 1.25% per month or fraction of a month from the date they were last payable without penalty. If the home was sold to a bona fide purchaser before the extra bill went out, the tax, interest, and penalties are not a lien on the property and are not billed to that buyer. Treasury assesses the former owner instead. That protection is one reason a seller should rescind promptly.

A land contract buyer has one more filing: Treasury says the buyer must file a Property Transfer Affidavit, Form 2766, with the local assessor within 45 days of the transfer.

More questions about Michigan Principal Residence Exemption

Does Michigan's exemption cover the whole property tax bill?

No. It removes the local school operating millage, up to 18 mills, from the bill. Millages other than local school operating still apply, so a bill drops but does not vanish.

Can I claim it on a cottage with a higher taxable value than my house?

No. Treasury says the exemption can be claimed only on the property that is the owner's true, fixed, and permanent home, and not on the basis of potential tax savings.

Do I have to file a new affidavit every year?

No. A valid claim stays on the property while the owner keeps meeting the requirements. A new affidavit is needed when a parcel is split or combined, because that creates new parcel numbers.

Who files the rescission when an owner dies?

The estate's personal representative or trustee files Form 2602 with the assessor within 90 days of death, because the deceased owner can no longer occupy the home or intend to return.

What if my trust owns the house?

The grantor or beneficiary who lives there signs Form 2368 in their own name, with the trust role noted. If the grantor cannot sign, the trustee may sign on the grantor's behalf, according to Treasury's claim guidance.

What the official sources say

  • State transfer tax exempt: instruments transferring property pursuant to or in lieu of mortgage foreclosure (not a subsequent transfer by the foreclosing entity). (MCL 207.526(v); source)
  • State transfer tax exempt: quitclaim deed to confirm title already vested/correct a flaw in title; judgments/orders of a court of record without specified monetary consideration. (MCL 207.526(l),(n); source)
  • County transfer tax exemptions include consideration under $100, leases, security instruments, court orders, boundary line instruments, and land contracts where legal title has not passed. (MCL 207.505; source)

What we could not confirm

Michigan transfer tax FAQ

What is the Michigan state transfer tax rate?

The statute cited above sets it at $3.75 per $500.

What does Michigan charge in transfer tax when a house sells?

A deed given for money triggers two separate levies. Michigan takes $3.75 for each $500 step of value, and any leftover amount counts as a full step (MCL 207.525(1)). The county adds 55 cents on that same step where it has fewer than two million people. Only the largest counties may authorize more, up to 75 cents (MCL 207.504).

Together the ordinary pair comes to $8.60 on each $1,000 of price. The step rule bites at the edges. A house that closes at $250,000 sits on exactly 500 steps, while $250,001 pushes it to 501 and adds $4.30. County charts print every bracket in turn for this reason.

Recording is the trigger. The deed or sale contract must display the total real property value, or carry an affidavit that does. When a sale bundles land with furnishings or equipment, only the real property is taxed, and only when the instrument lists the two values apart.

What is the seller's bill at common sale prices?

A $250,000 sale in a county charging the standard 55 cents costs the seller $2,150 in combined tax. The table runs the statutory rates against round prices. Midland County's published chart and Monroe County's fee page agree with these figures.

Combined Michigan transfer tax by sale price, using the state and standard county rates
Sale priceState taxCounty taxTotal
$100,000$750$110$860
$150,000$1,125$165$1,290
$200,000$1,500$220$1,720
$250,000$1,875$275$2,150
$300,000$2,250$330$2,580

Midland County's chart shows $860 for any price in the bracket ending at $100,000, which matches the first row. Monroe County states the same rates as $7.50 and $1.10 per $1,000.

Who ends up paying at the closing table?

The seller, called the grantor in the statute, owes the state tax. That is the plain text of MCL 207.523(2). Subsection (3) gives fifteen days from the day the deed reaches the buyer, with payment going to the treasurer in whichever county holds the parcel. Closing agents usually withhold the amount from the seller's proceeds.

A purchase agreement may assign the cost to the buyer instead. Whoever paid can request a refund from the Department of Treasury when the sale turns out to have qualified for an exemption, and subsection (4) reaches back four years. Read the cost clause in your contract and ask for an itemized settlement statement before you sign.

Which sales escape the state tax altogether?

Section 6 of the state act, MCL 207.526, runs through nearly two dozen exemptions. These come up most for homeowners:

  • A deed where the stated consideration is below $100.
  • A family deed handed down to a son, daughter, stepchild, adopted child or grandchild.
  • A quitclaim or other corrective deed that merely confirms title already vested in the grantee.
  • A foreclosure transfer or deed in lieu, with the lender's own resale taxed later.
  • A court judgment or order that sets no price.
  • A land contract that keeps legal title with the seller until the price is paid in full.
  • A deed forming a joint tenancy in which at least one joint owner already held the property.

Leases, security instruments, and spousal deeds that make or end a tenancy by the entireties also fall outside the tax.

Does the county tax follow the same list?

The county act is shorter. MCL 207.505 covers papers under $100, leases, security instruments, personal property interests, price-free court orders, boundary line fixes, title confirmations, qualifying land contracts, mineral rights and certain joint tenancies. It has no line for a deed to a child or grandchild and no general foreclosure exemption, though it does exempt foreclosures on government-backed loans.

A parent planning to deed a house to a daughter or son for token money should phone the county's recording office first and describe the exact deed.

What would a median-priced house owe in Midland and Monroe counties?

Taking the Census Bureau's mid-point home values, $195,400 for Midland County and $228,900 for Monroe County, as if they were sale prices, and counting $500 steps gives these results:

  • Midland County at $195,400: 391 steps, with $1,466.25 to the state and $215.05 to the county, for $1,681.30.
  • Monroe County at $228,900: 458 steps, with $1,717.50 to the state and $251.90 to the county, for $1,969.40.

The gap of roughly $288 between the two comes from the higher Monroe County price alone, because both counties levy the standard 55 cents. Local recorders confirm the final figure at the counter, and the title agent usually quotes it earlier.

Does the deed have to show the price?

Not always. Under MCL 207.525(2), an affidavit of total value can replace the printed price, using a form that Treasury prescribes. Midland County's recording page notes that a Real Estate Transfer Tax Valuation Affidavit lets the figure stay off the deed.

Both routes still produce a number for the tax math, and that number later reaches the assessor on the buyer's transfer affidavit. The deed, the affidavit and the settlement statement should all agree.

Is a land contract sale taxed differently?

Neither transfer tax reaches a land contract while legal title stays with the seller. Property tax law sees it differently. MCL 211.27a(6)(b) treats the contract itself as a transfer of ownership, so taxable value resets the calendar year after signing and stays put when the deed finally records.

If the contract carries a warranty clause, ask the treasurer's office for a tax certificate, because recording requires one.

How big is the recording side next to the tax?

Small. On a $250,000 sale the transfer tax is $2,150, against a $30 recording charge. A warranty deed also needs a tax certificate from the treasurer, which costs $5 for up to five legal descriptions in both Midland County and Monroe County. Beyond five, Midland adds $1.00 per description and Monroe adds $0.20.

The tax certificate and the transfer tax both go to the treasurer, so a seller with several parcels, such as a house plus an adjoining lot, should line up the descriptions early. Each extra description changes the certificate cost, and the combined value still sets the transfer tax.

What does the recorder charge on top of the tax?

MCL 600.2567 sets the recording charge at $30 per document, with no page count. Five dollars of it is routed to the automation fund. Documents that assign or discharge several instruments add $3 per extra, a plain copy runs $1 a page, and certifying one costs $5. Charter counties can adopt their own schedules by ordinance, so verify the figure locally.

Once the sale closes, the buyer has 45 days to send the local assessor the notice described in MCL 211.27a(10).

More questions about Michigan Real Estate Transfer Tax

Which rate does the state apply?

$3.75 for each $500 of value, rounded up for a partial step. That is $7.50 per $1,000 of price, set by MCL 207.525(1).

What does a typical county charge?

A county with fewer than two million people charges 55 cents per $500, or $1.10 per $1,000. A larger county may authorize up to 75 cents under MCL 207.504.

Is a deed from a parent to a child taxed?

The state tax exempts a conveyance from an individual to a child, stepchild, adopted child or grandchild under MCL 207.526(j) and (k). The county act has no matching entry, so confirm with the county's recording office before relying on it.

Do foreclosure deeds carry the tax?

The state act exempts a deed given in foreclosure or in lieu of foreclosure, though a later resale by the foreclosing entity is taxed. The county act is narrower, so confirm locally.

What is the flat recording charge for a deed?

$30 per document under MCL 600.2567, whatever the page count. Charter counties may set a different schedule, and each extra instrument assigned or discharged adds $3.

Michigan evictions are summary proceedings in district court.

What the official sources say

  • Summary proceedings may be used when a person holds over after termination of the lease under a power in the lease or implied by law. (MCL 600.5714(1)(c)(i); source)
  • Summary proceedings remedy is in addition to other remedies; judgment for possession does not bar other claims except as stated for land contract forfeiture. (MCL 600.5750; source)
  • A tenant holding over after termination of the lease under the lease or by law is subject to summary proceedings. (MCL 600.5714(1)(c)(i); source)
Selling in Michigan?
We buy Michigan houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • Whether a sale ends a lease.

How does an eviction start in Michigan?

No Michigan landlord may remove a tenant without the court. The landlord serves a written notice, waits out the notice period, and then files a summary proceeding in district court. For unpaid rent the notice is a written demand for possession, and the tenant has 7 days from service to pay or leave (MCL 600.5714(1)(a)).

The statute sets short clocks for these cases, measured in days. Owners planning a sale feel those clocks directly, since the court calendar decides when the keys can change hands.

The notice rule for rent is also stated in the landlord-tenant statute: when a tenant neglects or refuses to pay rent, the landlord may end the tenancy with a written 7-day notice to quit (MCL 554.134(2)).

Which notices does Michigan law recognize before a case is filed?

Several, and each one ties to a different reason for ending the tenancy. The notice has to match the ground the landlord relies on, so a landlord who sends the wrong one can lose time.

  • Unpaid rent: a written demand for possession, 7 days to pay or leave.
  • Controlled substance clause: a 24-hour written demand, but only where a formal police report has been filed.
  • Threat or injury to a person on the landlord's property: a 7-day written notice to quit, again tied to a police notification.
  • Serious health hazard or extensive damage discovered within 90 days before filing: a 7-day demand to hand back possession or repair.
  • Tenancy at will or by sufferance: one month's notice, or a notice equal to the rent interval if rent is paid more often than every 3 months.
  • Year-to-year tenancy: a notice to quit that ends the lease one year after service.

These grounds come from MCL 600.5714 and MCL 554.134. A tenant who stays after a lease ends under its own terms or by law also falls under summary proceedings.

How must a landlord deliver a rent demand?

Michigan Legal Help lists four accepted ways: hand it to the tenant, give it to a household member old enough to accept it, mail it by first class mail, or send it by email when the tenant agreed in writing and replied to a confirming message. The demand must describe the rental, state the rent owed, say the tenant has seven days, and show the landlord's address and the notice date.

Taping a notice to the door, sliding it under the door, or mailing it by a method that needs a signature are given as examples of improper service. If you are the owner and the service was done wrong, restart the clock with a fresh demand before you file anything.

What happens once the landlord files in district court?

After filing, the court issues a summons. Under the standard rule in MCL 600.5735, trial is set within 10 days of issuance and the summons must be served at least 3 days before trial. A court may adopt a local rule that sets appearance 5 days after service instead. The hearing is to happen within 7 days after the appearance or trial date, and it can be pushed back further only by stipulation of the parties or on the record.

For unpaid rent the landlord has to show three things: the rent was not paid, a proper demand was served, and the tenant neither paid nor left within the seven days. A tenant may answer that the rent was paid, ask for a rent reduction for poor repair, or file a counterclaim for repair costs.

A tenant can also apply for rental assistance before the first court date or within 5 days after it. With proof of the application filed and served, the case is paused for 14 days and can be extended once for another 14. Owners planning a sale should factor in up to four extra weeks when assistance is pending.

How soon can a court officer remove the occupants after judgment?

Usually not before 10 days have passed after the judgment for possession. That is the default under MCL 600.5744(5), and it matches the 10 days Michigan Legal Help describes for paying or moving out after a rent judgment.

The statute carves out faster paths. A writ can issue right after judgment, on conditions the court sets, when a unit was ordered vacated for lacking a required certificate of compliance, when entry was forcible or possession is held by force, when the occupant is a trespasser, when a serious health hazard or continuing damage is proven, or in the controlled substance case.

Slower paths exist too. After a land contract forfeiture, no writ issues for 90 days if less than half the price was paid, or for 6 months if half or more was paid. In rent cases, paying the judgment amount and taxed costs inside the window stops the writ. When the writ is carried out, the officer removes occupants and belongings and either leaves the belongings in an area open to the public or delivers them to the sheriff.

What does the typical timeline look like?

StageTime limitSource
Demand for possession served7 days to pay or leaveMCL 600.5714(1)(a)
Summons, standard ruleTrial within 10 days of issuance, served at least 3 days beforeMCL 600.5735(2)
Summons, local-rule optionAppearance within 5 days after serviceMCL 600.5735(4)
Hearing after appearanceWithin 7 days unless parties agree otherwiseMCL 600.5735(6)
Writ of restitutionNot before 10 days after judgment, with exceptionsMCL 600.5744(5)
Rental assistance pause14 days, extendable to 28Michigan Legal Help

Can an owner change the locks or cut utilities to speed things up?

No. MCL 600.2918 makes it unlawful for an owner to interfere with a tenant's possession by force or threat, by removing or keeping the tenant's belongings, by changing locks without handing over keys, by boarding up, by removing doors or windows, or by shutting off heat, water, or electric service the landlord must supply.

A tenant who proves interference can recover actual damages or $200, whichever is greater, for each occurrence, and can recover possession if it was lost. A person forced out in a forcible and unlawful manner can recover three times actual damages or $200, whichever is greater. These rights cannot be waived in a lease.

The owner is protected when acting under a court order, when making needed repairs or inspections as the law allows, or when in good faith believing the tenant has abandoned the home after diligent inquiry and with current rent unpaid. Suits to regain possession must start within 90 days, and damage claims within one year.

What changes when you sell a rented house in Michigan?

The security deposit stays an issue for the seller after the sale. Under MCL 554.614, a landlord whose interest ends by sale stays liable for the deposit until it is passed to the successor with written notice to the tenant by ordinary mail, until the successor meets the deposit rules, or until the tenant gets it back. Settle it in the closing papers and keep proof of the mailing.

The statute also lets a new owner recover possession by summary proceedings in two sale-related cases: occupants who stay after a mortgage or execution sale once the redemption time has run, and occupants who stay after a personal representative sells under probate court license or will authority (MCL 600.5714(1)(g) and (h)). Beyond those, whether a lease survives a sale depends on the lease text and the notices already served. Check with the clerk of the district court that covers the property, or with a Michigan attorney, before a buyer is told the house will be vacant.

  • Gather the lease, rent ledger, deposit amount, and any notice already served.
  • Pick the notice only after you know which ground applies.
  • Tell the buyer up front whether the house comes occupied or empty.

More questions about Michigan Eviction Process (Summary Proceedings) and Selling a Rented House

Is a 7-day notice enough to evict for unpaid rent in Michigan?

It starts the process but does not end it. After the 7 days run, the landlord must file in district court, win a judgment for possession, and wait for a writ, which normally cannot issue until 10 days after judgment (MCL 600.5744(5)).

Can I end a tenancy at will so I can sell?

Yes, through a notice to quit and then summary proceedings if the tenant stays. A tenancy at will or by sufferance ends on one month's notice, or a period equal to the rent interval when rent is paid more often than every 3 months (MCL 554.134(1)).

Does paying the judgment stop the eviction?

For rent cases, yes, if the full judgment amount and taxed costs are paid to the landlord within the time provided. A writ of restitution must not issue after that payment (MCL 600.5744(7)).

What if the tenant applies for rental assistance?

The case is paused for 14 days when proof of the application is filed and served, and the pause can be extended for 14 more days with a status update. Michigan Legal Help describes this process for nonpayment cases.

Who gets the security deposit when the landlord sells?

Until the deposit reaches the buyer and the tenant is told by ordinary mail who the new landlord is and where to write, or until the tenant is repaid, the seller remains liable (MCL 554.614).

What the official sources say

  • A conveyance worded 'A.B. quit claims to C.D.' (premises, consideration), signed, sealed and acknowledged by the grantor, is a sufficient quitclaim conveyance. (MCL 565.152; source)
  • Copies of records are $1.00 per page. (MCL 600.2567(1)(c); source)
  • Electronic documents under the Uniform Real Property Electronic Recording Act may be recorded where the register accepts them; electronic fee is due within 1 business day of receipt. (MCL 600.2567; source)
  • Recordable instruments must show each executing person's printed name beneath the signature, be legible, black ink on white paper, 8-1/2 by 11 to 8-1/2 by 14 inches, with a 2-1/2 inch top margin on page 1 and 1/2 inch margins elsewhere. (MCL 565.201; source)

Michigan quitclaim deed FAQ

Where do I record a Michigan deed?

With the register of deeds in the county where the property is located.

What makes a Michigan quitclaim deed valid?

A deed worded in substance as "A.B. quit claims to C.D.", with the premises described and the consideration stated, is a good and sufficient quitclaim conveyance once the grantor signs, seals and acknowledges it. That rule is in MCL 565.152, part of a statute dating to 1881.

The statutory wording is short on purpose. A quitclaim passes whatever interest the grantor holds and says nothing more, so it fits a transfer between people who already know the title, such as a spouse, a parent, or a co-owner buying out a sibling.

The form also leaves the price visible. Whatever consideration the deed recites feeds the transfer tax, the assessor's records and any later title review, so write the real figure, and keep that number consistent across every document you sign.

Names matter more than people expect. Spell every grantor exactly as the prior deed does, and list each grantee's mailing address, because the recording statute rejects a deed whose printed names disagree with the acknowledgment.

A signed deed is only the start. The deed still has to meet the recording rules, and the transfer may bring a tax filing, a transfer tax question and a change in the property tax bill.

What formatting rules must a Michigan deed meet to be recorded?

A deed that misses any item in the recording statute is refused for recording. The statute is MCL 565.201. Instruments executed after April 1, 1997 face the most detailed checklist:

  • A legible printed name under every signature, with ink that is black or navy, matching the name in the acknowledgment.
  • The grantee's address on the deed, with a street number where street numbers are in common use.
  • Who prepared the document, with that person's business address.
  • One line of text at the top that names the recordable event, such as the type of deed.
  • Blank space of 2-1/2 inches across the head of the first sheet, with half-inch margins on all other sides.
  • Print in 10-point type or bigger, dark ink, on white stock weighing no less than 20 pounds, sized from letter up to legal length.
  • Any Social Security number blacked out except its last four digits.
  • An English translation attached if any part is in another language.

The notary's printed name belongs beside the notary's signature on that same sheet. Check the checklist against your draft before driving to the county seat, because a rejected deed means a second trip.

Does a quitclaim deed carry Michigan transfer tax?

Often it does, because the tax applies to deeds given for consideration. The seller or grantor owes it, and payment is due at the county treasurer's office at most 15 days from the handover of the deed, per MCL 207.523.

Two layers apply. State tax runs $3.75 per $500 block of value, rounded up for any partial block (MCL 207.525). The county levy is 55 cents a block where the population is under 2,000,000, and a county above that size may authorize up to 75 cents (MCL 207.504). Either the deed itself states the full value being transferred, or a value affidavit travels with it. When real and personal property are sold together, only the land and buildings are taxed if the values are shown separately.

Ask the treasurer's office or the recording office which value affidavit to attach, and which of the two offices collects the tax at the counter in your county.

Which quitclaim deeds escape Michigan transfer tax?

The state act lists the exemptions in MCL 207.526, and the county act in MCL 207.505 has a shorter list. The ones that matter for quitclaim deeds are below.

Common transfer tax exemptions for deeds in Michigan
SituationExempt?Source
Re-confirming title the grantee already holds, such as correcting a defectYesMCL 207.526(n); 207.505(l)
Individual conveying to a son, daughter, stepchild or adopted childYes (state tax)MCL 207.526(j)
Individual conveying to a grandchild, step-grandchild or adopted grandchildYes (state tax)MCL 207.526(k)
Spouses creating or ending an entireties tenancyYesMCL 207.526(i); 207.505(i)
New joint tenancy where one of the joint owners already owned the landYesMCL 207.526(r); 207.505(o)
Consideration under $100YesMCL 207.526(a); 207.505(a)

If the tax was paid and the transfer later turns out to have qualified, the seller, or a buyer who paid on the seller's behalf, may ask Treasury for a refund in the form and manner it sets. The statute reaches back four years for transfers that qualify.

Where does the signed deed go, and what is the fee?

Bring the signed deed to the recording office serving the parcel's county. Under MCL 600.2567 the office charges a flat $30 to enter and record a document, regardless of length. Certifying a recorded document adds $5, and plain copies run $1.00 a page. A charter county may set its own schedule, so verify the amount before you go.

Where the register accepts electronic recording under the Uniform Real Property Electronic Recording Act, payment is expected a business day after the file is received, which is a different clock from the counter rule.

Recording protects the new owner. An unrecorded conveyance loses to a later good-faith purchaser who gave value and got a deed on the record first. The fact that the first recorded deed is a quitclaim does not by itself put that purchaser on notice of the earlier one (MCL 565.29).

How does a quitclaim deed affect the property tax bill?

A deed is a transfer of ownership under MCL 211.27a, and the grantee owes the local assessing office a notice inside 45 days. In the following calendar year, taxable value normally jumps to the state equalized figure.

Transfers of residential property to the transferor's or spouse's parent, child, brother, sister or grandchild are excluded from the definition, provided the home is not put to commercial use afterward. A transfer between spouses is excluded too. Even so, the filing is worth confirming with the assessor, because a missing filing on a taxable transfer carries a $5 daily penalty with a $200 cap for a principal residence, plus back taxes. Our page on the Michigan Property Transfer Affidavit walks through the deadline and penalties.

When is a quitclaim deed the wrong tool for selling a house?

The statutory form names a grantor, a grantee, the premises and the consideration. It contains no promise about what interest the grantor actually holds, so the form alone tells a buyer nothing about liens, missed heirs or unpaid taxes.

That gap matters in a sale at market price. Before signing, find out what is already recorded against the parcel and whether any taxes are unpaid. Have a Michigan attorney review any transfer that involves a loan, a divorce, an estate or more than one co-owner, because the deed does not change the loan agreement or settle who else claims an interest.

More questions about Michigan Quitclaim Deed

Which office records a Michigan quitclaim deed?

The register of deeds serving the parcel. A charter county may set its own fee schedule, and the default under MCL 600.2567 is $30 a document.

Is a quitclaim deed to my child exempt from transfer tax?

The state transfer tax exempts a conveyance from an individual to that individual's child, stepchild or adopted child (MCL 207.526(j)). Grandchildren are covered by subsection (k). Ask the county treasurer how the county tax exemption is claimed.

What happens if I never record the deed?

It becomes void against a later good-faith buyer who pays value and records first (MCL 565.29). Record soon after signing.

How soon must the transfer tax be paid?

Fifteen days from handover of the deed, paid to the parcel's county treasurer. The grantor carries the liability.

Does the new owner have to tell the assessor?

Yes, in most cases. The grantee must notify the local assessing office within 45 days of a transfer of ownership, and excluded transfers such as those between spouses are still worth raising with the assessor.

What we could not confirm

  • Treatment of a home sale gain and the federal exclusion.

Michigan capital gains tax FAQ

Does Michigan have a separate capital gains tax?

We confirmed only the flat individual income tax rate, from a search excerpt.

Is a home sale gain taxed by Michigan?

Yes. Michigan runs no separate capital gains schedule, so profit on a house lands in the same state income tax that reaches wages and other income. For the 2026 tax year the state rate is a flat 4.25 percent, which Michigan Treasury confirmed in an April 15, 2026 announcement after its yearly review of the rate.

The practical result for a Michigan seller is simple. Whatever part of your gain is taxable lands on your Michigan return at that one rate. Ask Treasury or a tax preparer how the federal exclusion carries onto the MI-1040 for your sale.

The rate is set by a formula in state law that Treasury, the Senate Fiscal Agency and the House Fiscal Agency run after each year's financial report is published. Treasury's 2026 notice says general fund revenue fell 1.56 percent in the fiscal year ended September 30, 2025 while inflation ran 2.70 percent, so no reduction was triggered. A court decision in 2024 held that any cut triggered by that formula lasts only one year.

How much of a Michigan home sale gain can be excluded?

IRS Topic 701 allows a single seller to exclude as much as $250,000 of gain on a main home, and a married couple filing together as much as $500,000. Check this exclusion before you estimate any state tax.

Two tests apply, both measured over the five years that end on the closing date:

  • Ownership: you or your spouse held title for 24 months or more.
  • Use: the house was your residence for 24 months or longer, and on a joint return each spouse must satisfy this one personally.
  • Look-back limit: a sale in the prior two years that already used the exclusion usually blocks a second claim.

The two 24-month periods may sit in different stretches of time. Each only has to land inside that single five-year window. IRS Publication 523 holds the full eligibility rules, the worksheets and the exceptions to the two-year rule.

What should a Michigan seller report to the IRS and the state?

A Form 1099-S from the closing agent obliges you to put the sale on your return, even when the exclusion wipes out every dollar of gain. A gain above the exclusion also has to be reported.

  • Use Schedule D and Form 8949 when the sale has to be reported.
  • A contract that pays you in later years makes the deal an installment sale, reported by the installment method unless you elect out. The exclusion stays available on those sales.
  • Uniformed Services, Foreign Service and intelligence community staff on qualified extended duty may pause the five-year clock for as long as a decade.

On the Michigan side, Treasury's tax year 2025 guidance lists a senior interest, dividend and capital gain limit of $14,688 for single filers and $29,376 for joint filers. Whether you qualify depends on your age and filing details, so check the current MI-1040 instructions or ask Treasury before you rely on it for a home sale.

What are the key Michigan figures for a house sale gain?

This table collects the numbers that matter when a Michigan owner estimates tax on a sale. Figures come from the IRS and Michigan Treasury pages listed in the sources.

Federal and Michigan figures for Michigan home sale gains, from IRS Topic 701 and Michigan Treasury
ItemFigureSource
Michigan income tax rate, 2026 tax year4.25%Michigan Treasury, April 15, 2026
Federal exclusion, single filerUp to $250,000IRS Topic 701
Federal exclusion, joint returnUp to $500,000IRS Topic 701

Michigan senior interest, dividend and capital gain limit, tax year 2025$14,688 single, $29,376 jointMichigan Treasury, tax year 2025 guidance
Michigan personal exemption, tax year 2025$5,800Michigan Treasury, tax year 2025 guidance

Do other Michigan taxes apply when the house sells?

Yes, though these charges attach to the deed and ignore your profit. Michigan layers a state deed tax (MCL 207.525) and a county deed tax (MCL 207.504) over the sale price, and both statutes name the seller as the party who owes them.

Deed tax follows the sale price, while income tax follows the gain. An owner who bought at $180,000 and sold at $230,000 pays deed tax on the full $230,000 even if the whole gain is excluded. Our Michigan closing costs page walks through the deed taxes and recording fee in detail.

How long can a Michigan seller amend a return that missed a home sale?

A taxpayer has 4 years from the due date of the original return to file and claim a refund with Michigan Treasury, according to its tax year 2025 guidance. Treasury's example is that a 2021 return and any homestead property tax credit claim had to be filed on or before April 18, 2026.

That window works in both directions for a seller. If you sold in an earlier year, left the sale off a return and later learn part of the gain was excludable, you have a limited time to claim a refund. If you owe tax, do not wait for the window to close. Since November 12, 2025, Michigan Treasury eServices has handled free filing of the state return, online payments, refund status checks and replies to Treasury letters in one place.

The same guidance lists a Michigan homestead property tax credit with a maximum taxable value of $165,400 and a credit limit of $1,900 for tax year 2025. If you sold partway through a year, ask Treasury how that affects a credit claim.

What if the Michigan house was inherited, rented out or owned for a short time?

The two-year tests decide most of these cases. A house you inherited and never lived in does not meet the use test, so the main home exclusion generally will not apply to its sale. A house you lived in for only part of the ownership period may still pass if you used it as your residence for 24 months inside the last five years.

For inherited property, the IRS requires that a recipient's basis in certain property from a decedent match the value finally determined for federal estate tax purposes. That rule comes from Internal Revenue Code sections 6035 and 1014(f) and applies when the estate had to file an estate tax return. Ask the estate's personal representative whether a Form 8971 statement was issued to you.

A seller who rented the property for part of the time should ask a tax preparer about depreciation and how the use test applies. Publication 523 covers those cases, and Michigan Treasury answers state filing questions.

More questions about Michigan Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Does Michigan have a separate capital gains tax?

No. A home sale gain is taxed at the state's single individual rate, fixed by Treasury at 4.25 percent for 2026. No extra state schedule exists for real estate gains.

Is the federal home sale exclusion honored in Michigan?

This exclusion is a federal rule, and Michigan Treasury sets the state return. Read the current MI-1040 instructions or ask Treasury how an excluded gain is entered.

Do I owe Michigan tax after living in the house under two years?

Possibly, since the federal exclusion wants 24 months of ownership and 24 months of use in the last five years. IRS Publication 523 lists exceptions to the two-year rule.

Will I receive a 1099-S after closing a Michigan sale?

Often yes. Often. A recipient of that form must report the sale on a return, even if the gain is entirely excludable. Ask the closing agent whether one will be filed for yours.

Does the buyer pay the Michigan transfer tax?

The statute names the seller or grantor as liable. A purchase contract can move the cost, so read the closing statement before signing.

Michigan land contracts have forfeiture and possession rules set by statute.

What the official sources say

  • Possession may be recovered by summary proceedings after forfeiture of a land contract only if the contract expressly provides for termination/forfeiture for nonpayment or other material breach; accelerated indebtedness does not count as money required to be paid. (MCL 600.5726; source)
  • A judgment for possession after forfeiture of a land contract merges and bars claims for money payments due at trial; a writ of restitution also bars claims for payments that would later become due. (MCL 600.5750; source)
  • State transfer tax exempt: land contract where legal title does not pass until total consideration is paid. (MCL 207.526(o); source)

What we could not confirm

  • Forfeiture notice periods under MCL 600.5728.

Michigan land contract FAQ

How is a land contract forfeited in Michigan?

See the statutes cited above and confirm the notice periods with an attorney.

What is a land contract in Michigan, and why does it matter when you sell?

A Michigan land contract is an installment sale: the buyer (the vendee) pays the seller (the vendor) over time and takes possession now, while the vendor keeps legal title until the contract is paid. Because title stays split from possession, a house under a land contract cannot be sold the way an ordinary owner-occupied home is, and every move depends on which side of the contract you are on.

The contract's own wording drives most outcomes. State law adds a few fixed rules about forfeiture, court timelines, taxes and recording, and those rules are the subject of this page. They come from the Revised Judicature Act, the Land Contracts act and the General Property Tax Act, all posted on the Michigan Legislature website.

  • A vendor who wants out can sell the right to future payments, pay off the buyer's side, or take the property back through forfeiture or foreclosure.
  • A vendee who wants out can assign the contract, pay it off with new financing and take a deed, or hand the property back.
  • A third-party buyer, including one paying cash, must find out who holds title and what is owed before offering anything.

How does a vendor forfeit a Michigan land contract?

A vendor can recover possession by summary proceedings only when the contract itself provides for termination or forfeiture after nonpayment or another material breach (MCL 600.5726). If the contract is silent on forfeiture, that route is closed. The same section says accelerated indebtedness does not count as money required to be paid, so a vendor cannot declare the whole balance due and then forfeit over it.

Before any court filing, the vendee must be served with a written notice of forfeiture (MCL 600.5728). The notice has to name the parties, give the contract date and the address or legal description, list the unpaid amounts with their due dates, and list any other material breaches. It must be dated and signed by the vendor, an attorney or an agent.

The vendee then has 15 days to pay what is owed and cure other breaches, unless the parties agreed in writing to a longer period. If the vendee does neither, the vendor may file for possession in court.

How long can a vendee stay after a court orders possession?

The wait depends on how much of the price has been paid. Under MCL 600.5744(4), a writ of restitution after a forfeiture judgment cannot issue until 90 days have passed if less than half the purchase price is paid, or six months if half or more is paid.

A vendee can still stop the process by paying the judgment amount plus taxed costs, and by curing any other material breach, within that window. Once a writ does issue, the same statute says the vendee's equitable right of redemption is cut off. That makes the writ date the real deadline for anyone trying to save the contract or sell their interest.

  • Under half paid: 90 days after the judgment before a writ can issue.
  • Half or more paid: six months after the judgment.
  • Payment of the judgment sum and costs, plus cure of other breaches, blocks the writ.

What happens to unpaid money after a forfeiture judgment?

Forfeiture is a trade: the vendor gets the property back and gives up the money claim. MCL 600.5750 says a judgment for possession after forfeiture merges and bars any claim for payments due or in arrears at the time of trial. If a writ of restitution issues, claims for payments that would have come due later are barred as well.

The vendor keeps a separate right to damages from the time of the notice of forfeiture. What happens to payments the vendee already made is a question for the contract and the court, because these sections do not set a refund rule.

Vendors who would rather collect the debt than recover the house can ask the circuit court to foreclose the land contract, since the circuit court has jurisdiction to foreclose mortgages and land contracts under MCL 600.3101. Any surplus from a sale under a foreclosure judgment goes to the court for the defendant or whoever is entitled to it (MCL 600.3135).

Can either side mortgage or borrow against a land contract interest?

Yes. The Land Contracts act lets a vendor or a vendee grant a land contract mortgage to secure any debt that a real estate mortgage could secure (MCL 565.357). It treats the vendor's right to payments and the vendee's right to a conveyance as real property interests. The same section keeps in force any contract clause that bars or defaults a mortgage, sale or assignment, so a due-on-sale style clause in the contract still counts.

A land contract mortgage is signed, acknowledged and recorded the same way as a real estate mortgage, and a recorded one is perfected without a separate commercial-code filing (MCL 565.358). For a seller this means a title search on a contract property may show liens against either party's interest, not just against the vendor's deed.

Which taxes and recording steps apply to a land contract sale?

For property tax, the General Property Tax Act treats a land contract as a transfer of ownership. Under MCL 211.27a(6)(b), taxable value is reset to the state equalized value for the year after the contract is signed, and it is not reset a second time when the deed is later recorded. The buyer has to notify the local assessor of the transfer within 45 days on the State Tax Commission form.

For the state transfer tax, MCL 207.526(o) exempts a land contract in which legal title does not pass until the full price is paid. The deed given at payoff is a separate document, so ask the register of deeds in the county what is due at that stage.

How should you sell a house that is under a Michigan land contract?

Start by pulling the signed contract, the payment history and any recorded memorandum or mortgage from the register of deeds in the county where the house sits. Those papers tell you who can convey what, how much is still owed, and whether a default is already on the clock.

  • Vendors: confirm whether the vendee is current, whether the contract allows forfeiture, and whether a payoff or a negotiated assignment is faster than a court case.
  • Vendees: ask the vendor in writing for a payoff figure, and check the contract for limits on assigning your interest before you market the property.
  • Heirs of either party: the person's interest in the contract passes to devisees or heirs subject to estate administration, so the probate rules apply before anyone signs a deed.
  • Buyers: expect the closing to include a payoff to the vendor, release of any land contract mortgage, and a deed from whoever holds record title.

A forfeiture case narrows the time available. A vendee, or a buyer stepping into the vendee's position, who pays the judgment sum and costs and cures other breaches inside the 90-day or six-month window stops the writ and keeps the contract alive.

More questions about Michigan Land Contracts

How many days does a Michigan land contract buyer get to cure after a forfeiture notice?

Fifteen days, unless the parties agreed in writing to a longer period. The 15 days run from service of the written notice, and the notice must itself declare forfeiture effective at the end of that period.

Can a vendor forfeit a land contract if the contract never mentions forfeiture?

No. MCL 600.5726 allows summary proceedings only when the contract expressly provides for termination or forfeiture, or gives the vendor the right to declare one, after nonpayment or another material breach.

How long before a writ of restitution issues after a land contract judgment?

It depends on payments made. A writ cannot issue until 90 days after judgment if less than 50 percent of the price is paid, or six months after judgment if 50 percent or more is paid. Paying the judgment amount and costs and curing other breaches inside that time blocks the writ.

Does a land contract change the property tax on a Michigan house?

It can. A land contract counts as a transfer of ownership, so the taxable value is reset to the state equalized value for the following year. The buyer must notify the local assessor within 45 days of the transfer.

Can a land contract buyer sell the house before paying it off?

Often yes, but the contract controls. Check for clauses limiting assignment or sale, get a written payoff from the vendor, and make sure the vendor's title and any land contract mortgage are cleared at closing so the new buyer receives a deed.

Michigan estate tax FAQ

Does Michigan have an estate tax?

We could not confirm a state estate tax rule on an official page, so we do not state one.

Does Michigan still have an inheritance tax?

Only for old estates. Michigan Treasury says the inheritance tax remains in effect solely for people who inherited from someone who died on or before September 30, 1993. If the person whose house you are selling died after that date, the Michigan inheritance tax does not apply to what you received.

Treasury defines an inheritance tax as a tax on the right to receive property by inheritance. That separates it from an estate tax, which is charged on the estate itself before assets are handed out.

When would a Michigan estate still owe the old inheritance tax?

Treasury's FAQ describes three situations in which an old estate can still need a tax determination. In each one the sender must write to Treasury within 90 days of the triggering event.

  • Estate reopened for a later-found asset: a probate estate is reopened because an asset turned up after the estate closed. Treasury wants the discovery date, the type of asset and its date-of-death value.
  • First-time probate where an asset appears: the letter gives the same facts, plus the petition to commence proceedings and the probate inventory.
  • Trust with deferred tax: when a life beneficiary dies and the trustee must make final distributions, the trustee reports the beneficiary's date of death and a breakdown of the remaining beneficiaries and their relationship to the original decedent.

If the asset is real estate, Treasury also asks for a statement from the local community showing the state equalized value as close to the date of death as possible. Include the will or trust agreement with every letter.

Where do I send inheritance tax questions in Michigan?

Mail them to the Michigan Department of Treasury, Inheritance Tax Section, Austin Building, 430 W Allegan St., Lansing, MI 48922. Treasury lists (517) 636-4419 as the contact number for the section. Keep the letter factual and attach the documents Treasury names, since the section decides from the file.

Most sellers will never need this office. It matters only when the person who died did so on or before September 30, 1993, and a property or asset from that estate is still unresolved.

What federal estate tax limit applies to a house passed on in Michigan?

For a death in 2026 the federal basic exclusion amount stands at $15,000,000, up from the prior year under a law signed July 4, 2025. An estate below that amount generally owes no federal estate tax, so an estate under it owes nothing at the federal level. The table shows the recent amounts published by the IRS.

Federal basic exclusion amount by year of death, from the IRS estate and gift tax page
Year of deathBasic exclusion amount
2023$12,920,000
2024$13,610,000
2025$13,990,000
2026$15,000,000

A surviving spouse can elect, on a timely filed return for the decedent, to take over any unused part of the exclusion. The IRS calls this portability. The yearly gift exclusion is $19,000 per recipient in 2026.

What tax paperwork follows an inherited Michigan house?

An estate that must file Form 706 also owes a statement on Form 8971 to the IRS and to each person who receives property. The statement lets a beneficiary match their basis to the value finally set for federal estate tax purposes. If the estate did not have to file a return, the IRS asks that no Form 8971 be sent.

  • The IRS closing letter user fee went from $56 to $76 on October 26, 2026.
  • The IRS publishes steps for getting an estate tax transcript in place of a closing letter, and the Transcript Delivery Service is open to authorized practitioners.
  • Gain on a later sale of the house is a different subject. It is covered on our Michigan capital gains page.

How does inheriting a house change Michigan property tax?

MCL 211.27a(6)(f) lists a conveyance under a will, or by intestacy, as a transfer of ownership. The taxable value then jumps to the state equalized value the following year. That can raise the bill noticeably if the old taxable value had been held down by the annual cap.

The reset does not happen when the heir is the decedent's spouse. Since December 31, 2014 it also does not happen for residential property passed to the decedent's or spouse's mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, adopted child, grandson or granddaughter, as long as the property is not used for any commercial purpose afterward. Treasury or the assessor can ask for proof of the relationship, and the heir has 30 days to supply it or face a $200 fine.

The new owner also owes the local assessor a notice of the transfer within 45 days.

Which Michigan offices should an heir call before listing the house?

Three local offices answer the questions that decide net proceeds. Each one holds records for the county where the house sits.

  • County treasurer: collects the county and state transfer tax and can say whether a family exemption applies to the deed.
  • Local assessor: receives the 45-day transfer notice and can tell you whether the taxable value will reset for the buyer or for a family member who keeps the house.
  • Recording office: files the deed at $30 under MCL 600.2567 and passes each recorded transfer on to the assessor.

The probate court for the county controls whether a personal representative has authority to sell. Bring letters of authority to the first call so the offices can see who signs the deed.

What basis rules follow an heir who sells the house?

The IRS issued final regulations on September 16, 2024 about consistent basis reporting between an estate and the person who acquires property from a decedent. They carry out a 2015 federal law that created Internal Revenue Code section 6035 and added section 1014(f).

Under section 6035 the executor of an estate that must file an estate tax return sends statements to the IRS and to each beneficiary. The heir's basis in covered property has to line up with the value finally set for estate tax. An heir planning to sell should ask the executor for that statement early, because the basis figure drives the gain reported on a later sale, as described on our capital gains page.

Does selling an inherited Michigan house trigger the transfer tax?

Usually yes, because the personal representative is the seller or grantor and the deed is for consideration. The state and county deed taxes, $3.75 and $0.55 per $500 in most counties, are explained on our Michigan closing costs page.

Two exemptions in MCL 207.526 can change the outcome. One covers a deed to a son, daughter, stepchild or grandchild, and the other covers a transfer made by court order where the court sets no dollar price. A deed to a child can therefore carry no state deed tax, while a sale on the open market is taxed.

MCL 600.5714(1)(h) also lets a buyer recover possession by summary proceedings if a person stays in a house sold and conveyed by a personal representative under probate court license or the authority of the will.

More questions about Michigan Estate and Inheritance Tax

Is there a Michigan estate tax I have to pay on a house?

Michigan Treasury's published inheritance tax FAQ applies only to deaths on or before September 30, 1993. For a later death, ask Treasury or the probate court about state filings, and check the federal limit of $15,000,000 for 2026.

How large is the federal exemption for someone who died in 2026?

The IRS basic exclusion amount for 2026 is $15,000,000. A smaller estate generally owes no federal estate tax, though a return may still be filed to elect portability.

Who do I contact about an old Michigan inheritance tax matter?

Write to the Michigan Department of Treasury, Inheritance Tax Section, Austin Building, 430 W Allegan St., Lansing, MI 48922, or call (517) 636-4419. Send the letter within 90 days of discovering the asset.

Will the tax bill rise after I inherit a Michigan house?

They can. Inheriting under a will or by intestacy lifts the taxable value to state equalized value, unless the heir is a spouse or a close relative who keeps the home residential.

Does a deed from the estate to my brother or sister owe deed tax?

A deed to a sibling is not on the list of family exemptions, which names children, stepchildren, grandchildren and step-grandchildren. A deed with consideration under $100 is exempt, so ask the county treasurer how a no-price transfer to a sibling will be treated.

  • Any official source describing a lady bird or transfer on death deed.

Michigan lady bird deed FAQ

Is a lady bird deed in the Michigan statutes?

We did not find one on an official page, so we do not describe how it works.

What is a lady bird deed in Michigan?

It is a deed in which the owner keeps a life estate and full power to sell, mortgage, or lease the home, while naming someone who receives it at the owner's death. Michigan's Department of Health and Human Services defines it in its Bridges policy glossary as an enhanced life estate deed, also called a transfer on death deed, that lets property pass on death without probate. The owner still owns the property and can sell, rent, or change it without restriction until death.

Michigan Treasury uses nearly the same picture in its principal residence exemption guidance. Its example has an owner deed the home to another person while reserving a life estate and full power to convey during life, including selling, gifting, mortgaging, leasing, or keeping the proceeds. Treasury names that arrangement a Lady Bird Deed.

The instrument still has to be a valid Michigan deed. The statutory short form for a quitclaim says a conveyance worded in substance as a quitclaim, signed, sealed, and acknowledged by the grantor, is a good conveyance to the grantee and the grantee's heirs and assigns (MCL 565.152). That form does not by itself describe a retained life estate, so the wording of the retained powers is what a Michigan attorney will draft.

How does the Michigan Medicaid program treat the deed?

Two different rules are in play, and both come from the state agency. On eligibility, the glossary says that because the grantor keeps unrestricted interest in the property, a lady bird deed is not considered a divestment when an applicant is in a divestment penalty situation.

Estate recovery is a separate question. MDHHS says it applies to Medicaid beneficiaries who are 55 or older and received long-term care services on or after September 30, 2007. The agency defines the estate as property passing to heirs through probate, but for someone who received an asset disregard from a long-term care partnership policy, recovery applies to all assets whether or not they pass through probate (MDHHS Estate Recovery).

The agency also defers recovery while a spouse, a child under 21, or a blind or permanently disabled child is living. An undue hardship waiver is possible for a home of modest value, meaning one worth less than 50% of the average home price in its county on the date of death, and the applicant must pass a means test of household income under 200% of the poverty level and household resources under $10,000.

MDHHS also warns that transferring assets to avoid recovery can affect eligibility, and that the law presumes no undue hardship when the hardship results from such a transfer (MCL 400.112g(3)(e)(iii)). Speak with a legal advisor before you sign a deed with Medicaid in mind.

Does a lady bird deed change the property tax exemption or taxable value?

It can affect who qualifies for the principal residence exemption. Treasury says a person who holds a life estate counts as a partial owner and is eligible if the home is their principal residence, and that any ownership interest must be in writing. In Treasury's lady bird example, the person named to receive the home has no current ownership interest because the grantor keeps full control, and becomes an owner only at the grantor's death if the grantor has not used the powers.

Taxable value is a separate issue. Under MCL 211.27a, a transfer of ownership uncaps taxable value in the year after the transfer. Subsection (6) defines transfer of ownership broadly, and subsection (7) lists transfers that are exempt from that definition. Treasury's change-of-ownership page says a transfer of ownership causes uncapping in the calendar year following the year of the transfer. Whether a particular deed, or the later death of the grantor, counts is a question for the local assessor.

What do the official sources say, side by side?

Michigan agency statements that bear on lady bird deeds

Can I still sell a Michigan house that has a lady bird deed?

If the deed keeps the full powers described above, the grantor is the person who sells. The MDHHS glossary says the owner may sell or rent without restriction until death, and Treasury's example lists selling, gifting, mortgaging, and leasing among the retained powers. A buyer's title company will still want to read the recorded deed itself, because a deed written with narrower powers changes who must sign.

  • Pull the recorded deed from the county register of deeds and read the retained powers.
  • Ask the title company whether it needs the named recipient's signature or a release.
  • If the grantor has died, the deed that names the recipient is the starting point, and the recipient should ask the assessor and the title company how the transfer is handled.

Michigan's simplified affidavit for small estates, court form PC 598, can be used only when no real property is in the decedent's estate, so a house is not handled through that form.

What happens to the exemption and taxes when the owner dies?

Treasury's claim guidance says a deceased owner is no longer eligible because the owner cannot occupy the home or intend to return. The estate's personal representative or trustee must file Form 2602, the Request to Rescind Principal Residence Exemption, with the assessor within 90 days of death. The exemption is removed as of December 31 of the year the rescission was filed.

The person who receives the home and lives there can claim a new exemption by filing Form 2368 with the assessor if they meet the ownership rules, by June 1 for the summer levy or November 1 for the winter levy (MCL 211.7cc(2)). A property transfer affidavit may also be needed, so ask the local assessor which filings apply to a transfer at death.

What should an owner ask before signing a lady bird deed?

The deed is a recorded legal document, and small wording differences control who owns what. Bring these questions to a Michigan attorney.

  • Which powers does the deed reserve: selling, mortgaging, leasing, and gifting?
  • Does the owner want a Medicaid planning result, and how does estate recovery apply if there is a long-term care partnership policy?
  • How will the county assessor treat the deed for uncapping and the principal residence exemption?
  • Who will file the rescission and affidavit forms after death, and within what time?

Call the assessor for the city or township where the home sits, and the register of deeds for the county, for their recording and filing requirements.

More questions about Michigan Lady Bird Deed

Does Michigan call it a lady bird deed in its official materials?

Yes, in two places. The MDHHS Bridges policy glossary lists Lady Bird Deed as another name for an enhanced life estate deed or transfer on death deed, and Treasury's exemption guidance uses the term in an ownership example.

Is a lady bird deed a Medicaid divestment in Michigan?

No, according to the MDHHS glossary. Because the grantor keeps unrestricted interest in the property, the deed is not considered a divestment when an applicant is in a divestment penalty situation.

Does the deed avoid Medicaid estate recovery?

Not necessarily. MDHHS says recovery reaches all assets, probate or not, for beneficiaries who received an asset disregard under a long-term care partnership policy, so ask a legal advisor how your facts apply.

Can the person named in the deed claim the principal residence exemption?

Not while the grantor keeps full control. Treasury says that person has no current ownership interest and becomes an owner only at the grantor's death if the powers were not used.

Does recording a lady bird deed raise property taxes?

That depends on whether the conveyance is a transfer of ownership under MCL 211.27a. A transfer of ownership uncaps taxable value in the next calendar year, so ask the local assessor before you record.
