What we could not confirm

  • Inflation adjustments to the small estate limit.

How does probate work when a Michigan homeowner dies?

Michigan handles estates under the Estates and Protected Individuals Code, known as EPIC. At death, a person's property passes to the people named in the will, or to heirs if there is no will, but it passes subject to creditors, family allowances and administration (MCL 700.3101). For a house, that usually means a probate court has to appoint someone with authority before a deed can be signed.

Probate runs through the probate court in the county where the person lived. The paperwork can be informal, handled through the court register, or formal, with a hearing. Informal is the lighter path and fits most estates with no dispute about the will or who should serve.

  • An informal application is sworn by an interested person and lists the decedent's details, the family members and the applicant's priority to serve.
  • A formal proceeding is required when anyone objects to who is appointed.
  • If a will exists, the original goes to the court with the application.

Who may serve as personal representative and sign for the house?

MCL 700.3203 sets a ranking. The person named in a probated will comes first, then a surviving spouse who is also a devisee, other devisees, the surviving spouse, and other heirs (MCL 700.3203). After 42 days a creditor's nominee can be considered, and after 63 days the state or county public administrator can step in if no interested person has applied, if no heirs are known, or if no heir is a United States resident entitled to a share.

Someone who ranks high can nominate another qualified person, or renounce in writing. Objections to an appointment can only be raised in a formal proceeding. Siblings who disagree about who should serve should expect a hearing, which adds time before any listing or sale.

An application for informal appointment is made by an interested person, and a creditor with a claim that cannot be enforced without administration may apply if nobody has filed within 28 days after death (MCL 700.3301).

Does the small estate affidavit work for a house in Michigan?

Usually not. The sworn-statement route in MCL 700.3983 requires the statement to say the estate does not include real property, and it covers tangible personal property, debts owed to the decedent and similar items, starting 28 days after death. It cannot move title to a house.

The court-order route is different. Under MCL 700.3982, a court may order property turned over to the surviving spouse, or to heirs if there is no spouse, when funeral and burial expenses are shown paid and the rest of the gross estate is $50,000 or less. Since 2024, a mortgage or other debt secured by real property in the estate is subtracted from its value, up to $250,000, when the court calculates that total.

The dollar figures are adjusted for inflation under MCL 700.1210. The Department of Treasury publishes the factor each year, so ask the probate court register or Treasury for the number that applies to the year of death. An heir who receives property by this order is responsible for the decedent's unpaid debts, up to the value received, for 63 days after the order.

What can a personal representative do about selling the property?

Once appointed, a personal representative may sell, mortgage or lease estate property for cash or on credit, including land in Michigan or elsewhere, unless the will or a court order says otherwise (MCL 700.3715). The same section lets the representative insure the property, make repairs and pay taxes and other costs of administration from the estate.

Within 28 days of appointment, the representative must notify heirs and devisees and the surviving spouse of the spouse's election rights (MCL 700.3705). Heirs who stay quiet about a sale can still be owed an inventory and an account later, so keep them informed before listing.

Special limits apply when the representative is the state or a county public administrator. The court must approve any sale of real property after a hearing, and fees tied to selling a property under tax or mortgage foreclosure are capped at 10 percent of net proceeds once those proceeds pass $30,000.

What if no one opens probate before the house is sold?

Michigan law does allow heirs and devisees to take an estate without administration. MCL 700.3901 says a successor can establish title by proving the decedent's ownership, the death and the successor's relationship. The catch is practical: a title company or buyer usually wants a court-issued authority, and the successor still takes subject to creditors' claims and family allowances.

Creditors have a defined window. If notice to creditors was published, claims arising before death are barred unless presented within four months of publication, and known creditors get one month after notice or the four months, whichever is later. If the notice rules were not followed, the window is three years after death (MCL 700.3803). A mortgage lender or lienholder is not affected by that bar, since the section leaves liens on estate property enforceable.

RouteWhat it coversSource
Sworn statementPersonal property only; estate must hold no real propertyMCL 700.3983
Small estate court orderGross estate of $50,000 or less after funeral costs, adjusted yearlyMCL 700.3982
Informal appointmentSworn application to the court registerMCL 700.3301
Sale by representativePower to sell land for cash or on creditMCL 700.3715

What steps should heirs take before listing an inherited Michigan house?

Work in order, because each step unlocks the next. A title company will ask for the court's letters of authority, and a buyer will ask who may sign.

  • Find the original will and the death certificate, and ask the county probate court which forms it wants for an informal filing.
  • Decide who will serve as personal representative, using the ranking above, and get any rival claimants to agree or renounce in writing.
  • Ask the county treasurer whether property taxes are behind, and ask the mortgage servicer for a payoff.
  • Keep the utilities on and the house insured while the estate is open, since the representative may insure and maintain the property.
  • Notify heirs and the surviving spouse within 28 days of appointment, then price and list the house.

An inherited house that passes to a child, parent, sibling or grandchild of the decedent may keep its capped taxable value for residential use. The property tax rules page explains how the uncapping rule treats family transfers.

More questions about Michigan Probate Process and Small Estate Affidavit for Selling Inherited Property

Can I sell an inherited house in Michigan without probate?

Rarely in practice. Heirs can establish title without administration under MCL 700.3901, but buyers and title companies usually require court-issued authority from a personal representative. The sworn-statement shortcut does not apply because it covers only estates with no real property.

What is the Michigan small estate limit for a house?

The statute states $50,000, adjusted for inflation under MCL 700.1210, and subtracts a mortgage on real property up to $250,000 when valuing the estate. The court-order route in MCL 700.3982 can reach a house, while the sworn statement in MCL 700.3983 cannot.

How soon must heirs be told after a personal representative is appointed?

Within 28 days. MCL 700.3705 requires notice to heirs and devisees, and to the surviving spouse about the right of election, no later than 28 days after the appointment unless a court rule sets another time.

How long do creditors have to make claims against a Michigan estate?

Four months after publication of the notice to creditors, or one month after notice to a known creditor if that is later. If the required notice was not given, claims are barred three years after death under MCL 700.3803. Liens on the property are not cut off.

Who decides who serves as personal representative?

The statute ranks the candidates: the person named in the will, then devisees, the surviving spouse, and other heirs. A court decides any dispute in a formal proceeding, and the public administrator can be appointed after 63 days if no one applies.

Michigan property transfer affidavit FAQ

Who files the Property Transfer Affidavit?

The buyer files it with the assessor within 45 days, according to the statute cited above.

What is the Michigan Property Transfer Affidavit?

It is the notice a new owner gives the local assessor after any transfer of ownership of Michigan real property. The duty comes from MCL 211.27a(10), which asks for a form prescribed by the State Tax Commission.

The form must state the parties to the transfer, the date of the transfer, the actual consideration paid, and either the parcel identification number or the legal description. The assessor uses it to decide whether the property's taxable value should reset for the following year.

A seller does not file it. Still, anyone who sells a Michigan house should know what the buyer must do, because the consequences of a missed filing can travel back to whoever failed to file on the earlier purchase.

Who files it, and with whom?

The buyer, grantee or other transferee files it with the assessing office of the local unit of government where the parcel sits. The statute names the local assessing office, so the city or township assessor is the one to contact.

The register of deeds helps the assessor from the other direction. Under the same subsection, the register notifies the local assessing officer at least once a month about recorded transactions that involve ownership, and makes recorded deeds available to the county tax or equalization department. A recorded deed therefore usually reaches the assessor anyway, but the statute still puts the filing duty on the new owner, and transfers that never get recorded depend on it entirely.

  • Filer: buyer, grantee or other transferee.
  • Where: the assessor for the city or township that contains the property.
  • Deadline: within 45 days of the transfer of ownership.
  • Contents: parties, transfer date, actual consideration, parcel number or legal description.

What counts as a transfer of ownership in Michigan?

The statute defines it as conveying title to, or a present interest in, property, including beneficial use whose value is substantially equal to the fee interest. A deed is the obvious case, and a land contract counts too. For a land contract signed after December 31, 1994, the taxable value adjusts for the year after the contract is signed, and recording the deed later does not trigger a second adjustment.

The list in MCL 211.27a(6) also reaches several transfers sellers sometimes overlook:

  • A conveyance to a trust, with exceptions when the settlor or spouse is the only present beneficiary.
  • A distribution under a will or by intestate succession, unless the heir is the decedent's spouse or a qualifying relative taking a residence that stays non-commercial.
  • A lease that runs more than 35 years including renewals, or one with a bargain purchase option.
  • A transfer of a tenancy in common interest, limited to the share conveyed.
  • A conveyance of more than 50 percent of the ownership of an entity that holds the property.

Which transfers are not a transfer of ownership?

Subsection (7) lists the exclusions. They include a transfer between spouses, a transfer through foreclosure or a deed in lieu until the lender sells the property, a transfer by court judgment or order without specified monetary consideration, and a transfer given as security.

Family transfers of residential real property are excluded when the new owner is the transferor's or the transferor's spouse's parent, sibling, child, adopted child or grandchild, and the home is not used for any commercial purpose afterward. Treasury or the assessor can ask the transferee for proof within 30 days, and a transferee who ignores the request faces a $200 fine. For this purpose a rental of fewer than 15 days in a calendar year does not count as a commercial use.

Even when an exclusion applies, ask the assessor whether a short filing is still wanted so the file shows why the taxable value stayed put.

How does a transfer change the property tax bill?

Each year the taxable value of a parcel is the lesser of two figures: last year's taxable value, minus losses, multiplied by 1.05 or the inflation rate (whichever is smaller) plus additions, or the current state equalized value. Assessment is at 50 percent of true cash value.

A transfer of ownership removes that protection for one step. Under MCL 211.27a(3), the taxable value for the calendar year after the transfer equals the state equalized value. After that, the annual limit applies again until the next transfer. Michigan buyers often hear this called uncapping, and it explains why a new owner's first full tax bill can be much higher than the seller's.

What if the buyer misses the 45-day deadline?

MCL 211.27b makes the assessor adjust the taxable value as if the transfer had been reported. The buyer then owes the extra taxes from the date of transfer, plus interest and penalty from the date those taxes would originally have been levied, plus a daily penalty that varies by property class.

Daily late-filing penalty under MCL 211.27b(1)
PropertyPenalty after day 45MaximumSource
Principal residence$5 per day$200MCL 211.27b(1)(d)(i)
Other real property, not commercial or industrial$5 per day$4,000MCL 211.27b(1)(d)(ii)
Commercial or industrial, sale price $100 million or less$20 per day$1,000MCL 211.27b(1)(c)(i)
Commercial or industrial, sale price above $100 millionFlat amount$20,000MCL 211.27b(1)(c)(ii)

The governing body of the city or township may waive the daily penalty by resolution. It cannot waive the back taxes. A buyer who disagrees can appeal the increase to the Michigan Tax Tribunal within 35 days of receiving the notice, but that appeal covers only whether a transfer happened and arithmetic errors, not the value of the home.

Can a missed filing follow the seller?

Yes, and this is the part that matters if you sold a house you once bought without filing. The levy is a lien on the property only while the non-filing owner still holds it. Once the property passes to a later buyer who did file, the earlier amounts are treated as the personal liability of the earlier buyer who failed to notify the assessor.

The state treasurer can act as collection agent for those personal amounts at the request of the local official and may keep up to 20 percent of what it recovers. If you bought a Michigan property and are not sure the notice was ever filed, call the assessor for the city or township before you list it and ask what the file shows.

How do you file the affidavit in practice?

Download the current form from the Michigan Department of Treasury or ask the city or township assessor for a copy. Fill in the parcel number from the tax bill or deed, the date title passed, and the actual price paid. Deliver it to the assessor within the 45 days, and keep proof of delivery.

Recording a deed is a separate step with its own cost. The register of deeds charges $30 to enter and record a document regardless of page count under MCL 600.2567, unless a charter county has set its own schedule. Ask the register for the current fee and the accepted delivery methods. Ask the assessor whether the office takes filings by mail, in person or online, since each city and township sets up its own counter.

More questions about Michigan Property Transfer Affidavit

Who has to file the Michigan Property Transfer Affidavit?

The buyer, grantee or other transferee does. The duty sits in MCL 211.27a(10), and the seller has no filing role, although a seller who bought without filing can carry personal liability for the earlier omission.

How many days does the new owner have in Michigan?

Forty-five days from the transfer of ownership. After day 45 a daily penalty starts, and the assessor can also adjust taxable value and bill additional taxes from the transfer date.

Is there a penalty cap for a family home?

Yes. For a principal residence the penalty is $5 per day up to $200. Other non-commercial property tops out at $4,000, and the local governing body may waive the daily penalty by resolution.

Does an inherited house need the affidavit?

Often it does, because a distribution under a will or by intestacy is a transfer of ownership. It is excluded when the heir is the decedent's spouse, or a qualifying relative taking a residence that is not used commercially, and the assessor may ask for proof within 30 days.

Does filing the affidavit mean the taxes go up?

A filing reports the transfer, and a real transfer of ownership resets taxable value to state equalized value for the next calendar year. An excluded transfer, such as one between spouses, leaves taxable value on the usual annual limit.

Michigan Tax Tribunal FAQ

What is the Tax Tribunal deadline?

The statute text above lists May 31 for some property classes. Confirm the deadline for your class.

What does the Michigan Tax Tribunal do for a property owner?

The Michigan Tax Tribunal is the independent body that hears disputes over property valuation, exemptions and special assessments once the local review has run its course. It sits apart from the Department of Treasury, the State Tax Commission, local governments and boards of review, and it hears each case fresh. Under MCL 205.735a(2), a proceeding there is original and independent and is treated as de novo, so the Tribunal does not simply rubber-stamp the board's number.

A homeowner in Michigan usually meets the Tribunal after losing at the March board of review, or after receiving a notice that a principal residence exemption was denied. For a seller, the appeal matters because the assessed number feeds the tax bill the next owner inherits. The Tribunal's own petition forms show the range of disputes it takes:

  • Valuation appeals over true cash value, assessed value or taxable value.
  • Poverty exemption and disabled veterans exemption appeals.
  • Other exemption appeals, special assessment appeals and classification appeals.
  • Non-property tax appeals, which have their own forms.

What has to happen before a Tribunal petition can be filed?

For residential property, the assessment must first be protested at the local board of review. MCL 205.735a(3) says the board stage comes before the Tribunal acquires jurisdiction, and a claim over a principal residence exemption goes to the July or December board of review first.

MCL 211.30 governs the board. Its first session falls on the second Monday of March, and a city or township can move the start to the following Tuesday or Wednesday by ordinance or resolution. That opening session starts between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m. and lasts six hours at least. During the full week the board owes taxpayers 12 hours of hearings, including three hours held after 6 p.m..

Anyone who files a protest is owed a written answer by the first Monday in June. It reports the board's action, the resulting state equalized and tentative taxable values, and the right to go on to the Tribunal, together with the Tribunal's address and the final filing date. A local unit may also allow residents to protest by letter.

What are the Tribunal filing deadlines by property type?

Classification of the parcel sets the clock, and the Tribunal says plainly that it cannot stretch a filing deadline. The July 31 date for tax year 2026 residential appeals has gone by, so a homeowner's next opening is July 31 of whichever tax year is under dispute.

Petition deadlines under MCL 205.735a(6)
MatterLast day to file
Residential real propertyJuly 31 of the tax year
Agricultural real property, timber-cutover real property, agricultural personal propertyJuly 31 of the tax year
Commercial, industrial and developmental real property; commercial, industrial and utility personal propertyMay 31 of the tax year
Other matters35 days after the final decision, ruling or determination
Contested tax bill (arithmetic errors only)60 days after the treasurer mails the bill

Timeliness is judged by the postmark, by hand delivery, or by the date a designated delivery service takes the package. If the final day lands when the Tribunal's offices are shut, the following business day counts. The statute also calls for certified-mail service on the respondent, with copies to the local school board secretary and, where the county is affected, its clerk.

How does a residential appeal run in the Small Claims Division?

Every residential property tax appeal can be filed in the Small Claims Division, which uses an informal process. Hearings are usually telephone calls of about 30 minutes before an administrative law judge or Tribunal member, and most owners speak for themselves. Property other than residential can join Small Claims when the tax in dispute is $100,000 or less.

The sequence after filing is short:

  • The Tribunal assigns a docket number and the local unit files an answer.
  • There is no discovery unless the Tribunal grants leave.
  • A notice of hearing arrives at least 45 days before the hearing.
  • Evidence must reach the Tribunal and the other side at least 21 days before the hearing, with a proof of service.
  • If a judge rather than a member hears the case, either side has 20 days to file exceptions to the proposed opinion, and the other side has 14 days to answer.

The Tribunal's page puts the time from filing to final decision at roughly 12 to 18 months, depending on docket load. If a hearing is not set until after the next April 1, the following tax year is added to the case automatically, which means evidence for both years may be due.

How do uncapping and a home sale affect a property tax appeal?

A sale resets taxable value for the buyer, so the old owner's capped figure does not follow the house. Under MCL 211.27a, taxable value is whichever is lower: last year's figure grown by the smaller of 5 percent or inflation, or the current state equalized valuation. Once ownership transfers, the next calendar year's taxable value jumps to the state equalized valuation.

Some transfers do not uncap the property. Examples include a move between spouses, a foreclosure up to the lender's resale, and residential property going to a parent, sibling, son, daughter or grandchild who keeps it out of commercial use. The new owner reports the transfer to the assessing office on the State Tax Commission form within 45 days, and recorders send assessors a monthly list of recorded transfers.

If you own a house with an appeal still open, ask the Tribunal or your assessor how the pending year is handled once title changes hands.

How do you file and reach the Tribunal?

E-filing is the Tribunal's favored route and needs an account registered to a working email address. Paper petitions go to P.O. Box 30232, Lansing, Michigan 48909, to 2407 N Grand River Ave, Lansing 48906 for other carriers, or by hand to 611 W. Ottawa St, Lansing 48933. Email and fax filings are refused.

A Small Claims petition has to include the notice behind the dispute: the board of review decision, an uncapping notice, or a principal residence exemption denial, for instance. Phone 517-335-9760 on weekdays between 8:00 a.m. and 4:30 p.m., except that nobody answers from noon until 1 p.m. The staff will not offer legal advice or opinions on whether to appeal.

Filed papers show up publicly in the docket lookup. Black out Social Security numbers, account numbers and other personal identifiers first. Owners may speak for themselves or send an attorney or other representative.

More questions about Michigan Tax Tribunal

When must a residential assessment appeal reach the Tribunal?

By July 31 of the tax year, under MCL 205.735a(6). The 2026 date has passed, so the next one is July 31 of the year you contest. Commercial and industrial real property follow May 31.

Is the March board of review mandatory for a home?

Yes for residential valuation or exemption disputes. The board stage, or the July or December board for principal residence exemption claims, must come first. Commercial and industrial owners may go straight to the Tribunal.

May an owner appear without a lawyer?

Yes. MCL 205.735a(10) allows a person to appear alone or with an attorney or another representative, and Small Claims hearings are informal enough that most owners speak for themselves.

What happens to an appeal if the house is sold?

Ask the Tribunal docket staff at 517-335-9760. The sale uncaps taxable value for the buyer in the next calendar year under MCL 211.27a(3), and the buyer sends the transfer notice to the assessor within 45 days.

How long until a Small Claims ruling arrives?

The Tribunal's page estimates 12 to 18 months from filing to final decision, depending on docket load, and its FAQ says Small Claims rulings typically issue within 90 days of the hearing.

Michigan closing costs FAQ

What does it cost to record a deed in Michigan?

The statute cited above sets the fee at $30 per document.

What closing costs does a Michigan seller pay by law?

The costs set by statute are two deed taxes and a recording fee. The state deed tax is $3.75 on each $500 block of value, and a leftover partial block counts in full. The county deed tax is 55 cents on each block, except in the largest county class, where the board of commissioners may set a rate up to 75 cents.

Commissions, title insurance, attorney charges and prorated utilities come from your listing agreement and purchase contract, so they vary from sale to sale. The statutory items above do not.

How do you calculate the Michigan deed tax on a sale price?

Divide the stated value by $500, round up any fraction to the next whole unit, then multiply by each rate. A $200,000 sale has 400 units. The state tax is 400 times $3.75, or $1,500, and the county tax at 55 cents is 400 times $0.55, or $220, for a total of $1,720.

The instrument has to state the real property's full value, or carry an attached affidavit that does. When land and movable items such as equipment change hands together, only the land is taxed provided the two values are listed apart. Treasury writes the affidavit form for the state tax, and the State Tax Commission writes the one for the county tax.

Who owes the Michigan deed tax, and by what date?

MCL 207.523 puts the liability on the grantor. Payment is made to the treasurer of the county containing the parcel, within 15 days after the deed is handed over. A closing attorney or escrow officer usually deducts the sum from your proceeds and remits it for you.

The purchase contract can move cost from one side to the other, so read each line of the settlement statement ahead of closing day. A buyer who pays the tax in the seller's place may also file the later refund request.

Which Michigan deeds escape the state tax?

MCL 207.526 names a long run of exempt instruments. These are the ones a house seller is most likely to meet:

  • A deed whose consideration is under $100.
  • A deed running from a parent to a son, daughter, stepchild or adopted child, and a deed running to a grandchild in any of those categories.
  • A spousal conveyance that sets up or dissolves a tenancy by the entireties.
  • A judgment or court order that directs a transfer and sets no dollar consideration.
  • A deed that results from a mortgage foreclosure or replaces one. A later resale by the foreclosing entity is taxed.
  • A corrective quitclaim that fixes a flaw in title the grantee already holds.
  • A land contract that keeps legal title with the vendor until full payment.

The county act, MCL 207.505, carries a similar list without the child and grandchild exemptions. Your closing agent should test the deed against both lists.

Can a Michigan seller recover deed tax already paid?

Sometimes. A seller, or a buyer who paid the tax in the seller's place, who believes the deed met an exemption on its signing date may apply to Treasury for money back. The refund right reaches transfers made in the four years before the amendment that created it.

One refund route is aimed at homeowners. Paragraph (u) of MCL 207.526 applies when the seller had claimed the principal residence exemption, the parcel's state equalized value had not risen above its value on the first tax day after occupancy or purchase (whichever came later), and the price was set by arm's length negotiation. Have your closing agent test the sale against that rule before the deed is signed.

What is the Michigan fee for recording a seller's deed?

MCL 600.2567 sets a flat $30 to record one document of any length. That one section also prices extras: $1 per page for copies, $5 to certify a recorded document, and a $5 floor on any records search at 50 cents per year searched.

A charter county can adopt a different schedule by ordinance or resolution, though it may not charge above its cost of providing the service. Phone the recording office for your parcel before mailing anything. An electronic filing must be paid for within one business day after the office receives it.

What do the deed taxes come to at several sale prices?

A few worked sales show how the block counting plays out in a county below the 2,000,000 population line, using the state rate and the 55-cent county rate:

  • $90,000 sale: 180 blocks. State $675, county $99, combined $774.
  • $125,000 sale: 250 blocks. State $937.50, county $137.50, combined $1,075.
  • $450,000 sale: 900 blocks. State $3,375, county $495, combined $3,870.
  • $200,250 sale: 401 blocks, because the extra $250 counts as a full block. State $1,503.75, county $220.55, combined $1,724.30.

Netting these against your payoff, commission and prorated bills gives a more realistic proceeds figure than the sale price alone. A seller whose deed is on the exempt list owes none of it, which can change the math on a family transfer.

How do land contracts and foreclosure sales change the costs?

Deed tax is waived on a land contract while the vendor keeps legal title until the price is fully paid (MCL 207.526(o)). Property tax runs the other way. A land contract signed after 1994 counts under MCL 211.27a(6)(b) as a change of ownership, which resets the taxable value in the following year. Recording the deed later does not reset it twice.

Paragraph (v) of the same section exempts a foreclosure deed or deed in lieu from the state tax, but not the foreclosing entity's own resale. A borrower behind on payments should ask the county treasurer how a chosen deed will be taxed before signing it.

What are the fixed Michigan seller costs at a glance?

Statutory Michigan seller closing charges and where each comes from
ChargeAmountStatute
State real estate transfer tax$3.75 per $500 or fractionMCL 207.525
County transfer tax, county under 2,000,000 people55 cents per $500 or fractionMCL 207.504
County transfer tax, county of 2,000,000 or moreUp to 75 cents per $500 or fractionMCL 207.504
Recording a document$30MCL 600.2567
Certifying a recorded document$5MCL 600.2567
Tax payment deadline15 days after the deed is deliveredMCL 207.523

What happens to property taxes when a Michigan house sells?

The grantee has 45 days to file a transfer notice with the local assessor, on a State Tax Commission form that shows the parties, date, actual price and parcel number. Separately, the recording office sends the assessor a list of recorded transfers at least once a month.

Under MCL 211.27a a change of ownership lifts the taxable value to full state equalized value from the following January. A transfer to a spouse does not trigger the reset, and since 2014 neither does a residential transfer to a parent, child, sibling or grandchild who keeps it non-commercial. The contract decides how this year's bill is split, and the settlement statement carries the proration line.

More questions about Michigan Closing Costs for Sellers

What would deed taxes total on a $300,000 Michigan sale?

Roughly $2,580 where the county has under 2,000,000 residents. Six hundred $500 units at $3.75 give $2,250, and at 55 cents they give $330 more.

Is the buyer or the seller responsible for the deed tax?

The statute names the seller, so the seller normally funds it out of proceeds. A purchase agreement may allocate it differently.

How much does Michigan charge to file a deed?

The statutory base is $30 per document, with certification priced separately. Charter counties may publish another schedule.

Does gifting the house to my daughter or son create deed tax?

Under MCL 207.526, paragraph (j) frees a deed to a son, daughter, stepchild or adopted child from the state tax, and paragraph (k) does the same for grandchildren. The county list in MCL 207.505 has no matching paragraph, so confirm the county side with the treasurer.

What is the payment deadline for the tax?

Fifteen days from delivery of the deed. Closing funds normally cover it.
